summary:
Hessen stands under Germany's national framework: identity documents, legal gender recognition and equality protection are set nationally and apply in this state without local variation. What follows covers only Hessen's own policing, courts, incidents and facilities.

Police-registered queer-hostile offences in Hessen rose from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023, to 135 in 2024 and to 141 in 2025, a more than fourfold increase within four years. Interior Minister Roman Poseck (CDU) described the development as alarming, and in a May 2026 answer to a Grüne Landtag inquiry called the recorded figure only the tip of the iceberg, given the high dark figure from victims who do not report. The 2024 total comprised 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult.

Enforcement outcomes are thin relative to the volume of reports. Suspects were identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions followed. Poseck attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces. Hessen police maintain dedicated contact officers for this hate crime, and LSBTIQ* liaison officers have been established in all police headquarters since 2010 under a governing framework concept; the state government states it will pursue prosecutions consistently.

The figures are raw counts with no per-capita denominator, so they show the direction and scale of reporting in Hessen rather than a measure of relative danger against other German states. The Federal Criminal Police Office's situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people notes that a new federal reporting category now makes state-by-state comparison possible but that classification changes can inflate individual state counts, so cross-state numbers need caution.

A January 2026 incident in Kassel, cited by Poseck, saw a male couple homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on aboard a tram.

At Frankfurt Airport, trans woman artist BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act after a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer during screening on 23 November 2024 and told her she was not a woman. Frankfurt Airport apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised training for security staff on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers.
tangentialFactors:
The rise in Hessen is part of a multi-year national increase in police-registered queer-hostile offences recorded by the Federal Criminal Police Office, published with the Interior Ministry. Hessen's trajectory mirrors that national direction rather than standing apart from it.

The Interior Minister's attribution of part of the responsibility to far-right forces places the recorded violence within a political context that a visitor may notice in public space, particularly around demonstrations and nightlife districts.

The gap between the 2024 and 2025 totals, 135 to 141, indicates the increase has continued rather than plateaued, though year-on-year movement of this size sits within the reporting and classification effects the Federal Criminal Police Office warns about.

The Frankfurt Airport complaint is one documented instance of differential treatment at screening in this state; the inventory contains no comparable accounts from other Hessen entry points, so its frequency cannot be assessed.
localsOnly:
Residents reporting anti-queer or anti-trans crime in Hessen can approach dedicated contact officers in the state police, a structure backed by LSBTIQ* liaison officers in all police headquarters since 2010 and a framework concept governing their role.

The conviction record sets expectations for those who report: six convictions resulted from the 2024 proceedings in which suspects were identified in 46 cases. The state government's stated commitment to consistent prosecution sits against that outcome.

The high dark figure means official counts understate the experience of residents, a point the Interior Minister himself made when characterising the 2025 total as the tip of the iceberg.

Residents at Frankfurt Airport have a documented route of redress through the Equal Treatment Act, as used in the November 2024 screening complaint, alongside the airport's own complaint channel.
outOfScopeNotes:
No per-capita or population denominator is available for Hessen's offence counts, so the totals cannot be converted into a rate or used to rank Hessen against other German states. The raw-count ranking caveat from the Federal Criminal Police Office applies.

The inventory contains no Hessen-specific material on prison placement for trans inmates, identity-document or marker rules, visa and entry screening beyond the Frankfurt Airport account, facilities access, or access to gender-affirming care in this state. Those layers are carried nationally.

The outcome of BASHKKA's complaint under the Equal Treatment Act, and whether the promised Frankfurt Airport staff training was delivered, are unresolved in the sources.

Whether the identified suspects and convictions in the 2024 proceedings involved trans victims specifically is not broken down in the available reporting; the counts aggregate queer-hostile offences.
